title: UK Perspectives 2016: Trade with the EU and beyond

breadcrumb.text: UK Perspectives 2016: Trade with the EU and beyond

body.text: One of the most contested aspects of the EU Referendum debate has been the potential impact on trade between the UK and the rest of the EU.

So, what can ONS statistics tell us about the importance of trade with and beyond the EU for the UK? This article is part of a series of [UK Perspectives](http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20170726163612/https://visual.ons.gov.uk/?p=7837&preview=true), on topics such as the economy and housing, as well as two new articles; this one and another on contributions to the EU budget.

body.h3: Q. How important is the EU to UK trade?
body.text: Q. How important is the EU to UK trade?

body.h3: Q. How important is the EU to UK trade?
body.text: The EU is a large market for the UK, particularly for our exports of services and goods, including components and fuels.

body.h3: Q. How important is the EU to UK trade?
body.text: In 2015, 44% of the UK's goods and services were exported to the EU, while 53% of our imports came to the UK from the EU.

body.h3: Q. How important is the EU to UK trade?
body.text: In the same year, UK exports to the EU were valued at £223.3 billion, while UK imports from the EU stood at £291.1 billion.

body.h3: Q. How important is the EU to UK trade?
body.text: For countries outside the EU, UK exports that year were valued at £288.2 billion, while imports were worth £257.1 billion.

body.text: UK exports to the EU have risen by 68% between 1999 and 2015 (when relevant trade statistics were first collected), while imports have risen by 101% (these figures are in current prices, so not adjusting for inflation).

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.text: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.text: Between 2012 to 2014 an average of slightly more than 50% of the UK’s exports of goods went to the EU and just under 50% to non-EU territories, primarily the USA and China.

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.text: Last year, goods exports to non-EU countries pulled ahead, with a 53% share of the total.

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.text: In 2014, the United States was the country with the single largest share of UK exports of goods and services, but seven of the UK's main trading partners are from within the EU (Germany, Netherlands, France, Ireland, Belgium and Luxembourg (combined), Italy and Spain).

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.text: In 2015, 11% of the UK’s exports of goods went to Germany, compared with 17% to the US, while 15% of imports of goods came from Germany, compared with 9% from the US.

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.text: The UK has increasingly been trading with emerging and advanced economies from outside the EU, with the proportion of trade with EU countries falling since 1999.

body.box_text:
What is the balance of trade?
 The UK runs a trade deficit in goods and a trade surplus in services with the EU.

The UK exports more in services than it imports, which means it runs a trade surplus for services. This is because the UK economy is now dominated by the service sector, rather than manufacturing and other production.

When we look at the UK’s trade in goods, however, we find that we import more than we export, which means we run a trade deficit for goods.

The surplus in the trade in services does not make up for the trade deficit in goods, so overall, the trade balance is in deficit

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: In 2014, the USA was the UK’s largest trading partner in services accounting for 23% of total UK exports of services and 18% of UK service imports. However, as with trade in goods, more than half of the UK’s top 10 trading partners in services are EU countries, with Germany, Netherlands, Spain and France dominating.

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: Within the EU, the UK exports the majority of its goods and services to a handful of countries - Germany, France, Ireland and the Netherlands.

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: This is partly because:

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: France and Germany are large economies and geographically close to the UK

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: Germany is an EU manufacturing hub that uses UK components

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: There are historical trade links with Ireland, and a common language

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: The Netherlands is a global gateway, through the port of Rotterdam, that acts as an intermediate destination for trade between the UK and other countries. This is known as the Rotterdam effect.[1](#footnote1) It’s also an important financial and business services trading centre.

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: The UK is also an important part of the EU supply chain, as a relatively high proportion of our exports of goods are components manufactured in the UK for onward assembly elsewhere in the EU.

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: For example, Airbus aeroplane wings are manufactured in the UK for export and onward assembly in other parts of Europe.

body.h3: Q. Who does the UK trade with in the EU and beyond the EU?
body.h4: UK top 10 trading partners in goods and services, current prices, 2014
body.text: The UK tends to export more components, fuels, food and beverages, and basic materials to the EU than non-EU countries, but export more finished goods and services to non-EU countries than to the EU.

body.h3: Q. How important is UK trade to the rest of the EU?
body.text: Q. How important is UK trade to the rest of the EU?

body.h3: Q. How important is UK trade to the rest of the EU?
body.text: While the EU market is an important destination for the UK’s exports and an important source of UK imports, the UK is a smaller player in terms of significance to the EU.

body.h3: Q. How important is UK trade to the rest of the EU?
body.text: This is partly because the EU is such a large market that any one destination for exports or source of imports will be relatively small compared to the total.

body.h3: Q. How important is UK trade to the rest of the EU?
body.text: The EU accounts for almost half of the UK’s exports, reflecting the fact it is such a large market, comprised of 27 other countries.

body.h3: Q. How important is UK trade to the rest of the EU?
body.text: However, the UK, as one of many trading partners, accounts for 4%-5% of all other EU countries’ imports – the other side of the UK’s EU export relationship.

body.h3: Q. How important is UK trade to the rest of the EU?
body.text: The UK is also a relatively small export destination for EU goods, accounting for 6%-7% of total exports of other EU countries over the past eight years.[2](#footnote2)

body.h3: Q. How important is UK trade to the rest of the EU?
body.text: The share of EU exports going to the UK has been gradually declining over the past 15 years, but it has risen marginally in the last four years. This may partly be due to strong growth in the UK economy or the strength of the pound against the euro in recent years, both of which may have led to higher UK imports.

body.h3: Q. How important is trade for the UK economy?
body.text: Q. How important is trade for the UK economy?

body.h3: Q. How important is trade for the UK economy?
body.text: The UK buys and sells goods and services across the world, in the form of imports and exports.

body.h3: Q. How important is trade for the UK economy?
body.text: Accessing markets beyond our shores helps the economy to grow and supports living standards. The UK is able to sell its goods overseas and in return can purchase goods that might be relatively cheaper, better quality, or offer a wider range of choice.

body.h3: Q. How important is trade for the UK economy?
body.text: Exports in 2015 made up for 27% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), whereas imports are equivalent to around 29% of the UK’s GDP.

body.h3: Q. How important is trade for the UK economy?
Q. How important is trade for the UK economy?
body.box_text:
What is GDP?
 GDP (Gross Domestic Product) represents the total value in £s of a country’s goods and services in a given period of time. It’s a way of measuring how well the economy is doing.

body.h3: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?
body.text: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?

body.h3: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?
body.text: As well as trading with other parts of the world, companies also invest overseas.

body.h3: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?
body.text: This is known as Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and comes in the form of:

body.h3: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?
body.text: Outward investment - by UK nationals and companies in overseas countries.

body.h3: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?
body.text: Inward investment - by foreign nationals and companies into the UK.

body.h3: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?
body.text: In simple terms, FDI can attract investment into the UK economy from overseas, while also providing UK investors with market opportunities elsewhere.

body.h3: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?
body.text: In 2014 38% of the total UK overseas investment stock (FDI), was in EU countries, whereas 25% was in North America. ([ONS, 2016b](http://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/nationalaccounts/balanceofpayments/articles/ananalysisofforeigndirectinvestmentthemaindriveroftherecentdeteriorationintheukscurrentaccount/january2016)).

body.h3: Q. What about investment into the UK or abroad?
body.text: The EU is also the largest investor in the UK in terms of FDI, accounting for 44% of total investment (FDI), followed by North America which accounted for 25%.
